subject: How to create a data frame with one column of fits?

messages.author: 8757f45da80a9e6c
messages.subject: How to create a data frame with one column of fits?
parts:
Hi,

I am attempting to create a large number of fit objects and store them as a column of a data frame where the other columns are parameters of the fits. The idea is that later I will use cast to get related fits on he same row of a different data frame so that I can calculate functions of the relation between fits. (They're not really fits but lists of functions.)

I have been trying things like:

# read a data file, fit one model, return a one row data frame with the fit and a parameter of the fit
get.1 <- function(filename) {
  param <- derive.param(filename)
  data.frame(param=param, fit=fit.model(filename, param))
}

# read all the files and return all the fits and their parameters as a data frame
get.all <- function() {
    files <- list.files()
    adply(files, 1, get.1)
}

All the variations I have tried either blow up with an error message (**ply is unable to construct the output) or the output created has a strange shape and isn't a data frame as I wanted.

Is it possible to do this at all? Are there some examples somewhere?

So far I suspect that I can't create a data frame with a column of fits. I'm thinking of creating two data structures: a list of fits and a data frame of fit parameters with one column being a set of indices into the list of fits. Any suggestions?

Thanks

On Thu, Nov 29, 2012 at 8:22 AM, Ross Gayler <r.ga...@gmail.com> wrote:
> Hi,
>
> I am attempting to create a large number of fit objects and store them as a
> column of a data frame where the other columns are parameters of the fits.
> The idea is that later I will use cast to get related fits on he same row of
> a different data frame so that I can calculate functions of the relation
> between fits. (They're not really fits but lists of functions.)
>
> I have been trying things like:
>
> # read a data file, fit one model, return a one row data frame with the fit
> and a parameter of the fit
> get.1 <- function(filename) {
> param <- derive.param(filename)
> data.frame(param=param, fit=fit.model(filename, param))
> }
>
> # read all the files and return all the fits and their parameters as a data
> frame
> get.all <- function() {
> files <- list.files()
> adply(files, 1, get.1)
> }
>

You probably want ldply() in the last line of the function rather than adply().

Here's a toy example. I have five small csv files named data[1:5].csv
in my current directory, each with two variables x and y. I create a
small function f() that reads in a data file, runs a linear model and
extracts the coefficients and R^2 value from each model, returning a
single data frame.

files <- paste0("data", 1:5, ".csv")
f <- function(x)
{
d <- read.csv(x, header = TRUE)
m <- lm(y ~ x, data = d)
# convert a numeric vector to a one-line data frame
cf <- as.data.frame(as.list(coef(m)))
names(cf) <- c("intercept", "slope")
cf$rsq <- summary(m)$r.squared
cf
}
ldply(files, f)
intercept slope rsq
1 0.8243074 0.7539069 0.8323205
2 -0.1097787 0.9652193 0.8953010
3 -0.4360433 0.9648074 0.8521443
4 -0.1851447 0.8001332 0.8894204
5 0.4046049 0.8614875 0.8756457

> adply(files, f)
Error in as.integer(.margins) :
cannot coerce type 'closure' to vector of type 'integer'

So think of the vector of file names as a list object wrt plyr. The
correct plyr function to use in this case is ldply() because the input
vector of file names should be interpreted as a list object and the
function f returns a data frame. This is the plyr equivalent of

# clist is a list of one-line data frames
clist <- lapply(files, f)
do.call(rbind, clist)

If you still get errors after this change, there is probably an error
in your function somewhere.

Dennis

parts:
Hi,

I'm cross-posting this to manipulatr as it adds information to the
earlier postings here and may be of use if someone finds this thread
by search.

Summary - I got a suggestion to use the hyperframe data structure from
the spatstat package, because it is an extension of the data frame
that allows columns with non-atomic values. Unfortunately, it doesn't
play nicely with plyr. So, I'll stick with my original conclusion to
use a data frame for storing model parameters and a list for storing
models and manually keeping the two in synch.

Ross

---------------------------------------------------

Hi Hong, Bill, Adrian,

I finally got time to look in detail at the suggestions made by Hong,
Bill, and Adrian.

I have included a rather long test script below, if you want to plough
through what I did.

The brief summary of my conclusion is: I'll continue with my current
approach of having a k-row data frame of parameters and a k-element
list of corresponding models and manually manage the correspondence
between the two.

The issue with Hong's suggestion of adding a list of models as a
pseudo-column to a data frame and Adrian's suggestion of using a
hyperframe (from the spatstat package) is that neither method
completely reproduces the data frame interface behaviour. For example,
with Hong's method df[1,"models"] returns a list of length 1
containing a model object rather than the model object itself.
Adrian's hyperframe does a similar thing: hf[1,"models"] returns a 1x1
hyperframe containing a model object, rather than the model object
itself. Also, other packages that I want to use (specifically, plyr)
fail or only workunder very specific circumstances when applied to
these data structures. My guess is that plyr is directly accessing
some of the data frame internals rather than only operating via the
data frame interface behaviour. If this is true, then even those cases
(of applying plyr to Hong and Adrian's suggestions) that do currently
work might fail if the implementation of data frame or plyr is
changed.

Moving on to Bill's suggestion of a doubly indexed list: so much of R
is set up for convenience when dealing with data frames that I would
probably spend a reasonable quantity of code converting subsets of the
columns of the doubly indexed list to data frames and back. So I think
it would be less effort to keep the two data structures I currently
use (data frame for parameters and list for models) in synch.

Thanks for all your help.

Ross

#####################################
library(plyr)

##### try it the way I am currently using #####
# data frame of parameters and a separate list of models (one per row
of the data frame)
df1 <- data.frame(a=1:3, b=4:6) # store the parameters describing some
populations to be modeled
model1 <- alply(df1, 1, function(p){n <- 100; x <- rnorm(n); lm(I(p$a
* x + p$b + rnorm(n)) ~ x)}) # generate a list of models
df1$model.i <- seq_along(model1) # store the indices of the models in the list
x1 <- list(params=df1, models=model1) # package the parameters and
models as a single object to pass around

# the elements of the parameters and models are accessible in the usual way
# but with the disadvantage of a level of indirection to get from the
parameters to the corresponding models
x1$params
x1$params[1,]
summary(x1$models[[x1$params$model.i[1]]]) # summarize a model
corresponding to a row of parameters

# typical function to use the models and parameters
fn1 <- function(x){
p <- x$params
m <- x$models
adply(p, 1, function(df){xx <- rnorm(50); yy <- (df$a * xx +
df$b)^3; zz <- predict(m[[df$model.i]], newdata=data.frame(x=xx));
data.frame(r=cor(yy, zz))})
}
fn1(x1)

##### try it the way hong ooi suggested #####
# insert a list of models as a column into the data frame
df2 <- data.frame(a=1:3, b=4:6) # store the parameters describing some
populations to be modeled
model2 <- alply(df2, 1, function(p){n <- 100; x <- rnorm(n); lm(I(p$a
* x + p$b + rnorm(n)) ~ x)}) # generate a list of models
str(model2, max=1) # the list has some attributes added by alply
str(list(1,2,3), max=1) # an ordinary list does not have those added attributes
df2$models <- model2 # store the list of models as though it is a column

# can we access the models as we would expect?
dim(df2) # ok
names(df2) # ok
df2 # FAIL "Error in unlist(xx) : argument not a list"

str(lm(I(rnorm(10)) ~ rnorm(10)), max=1) # an lm object is a list of 12
str(model2[[1]], max=1) # an lm object retrieved from a list is a list of 12

str(df2[1,3], max=1) # retrieve using [ returns a list of 1
str(df2[1,3][[1]], max=1) # returns a list of 12
str(df2[[1,3]], max=1) # retrieve using [[ returns a list of 12
df2[1,1] # ok
df2[[1,1]] # ok
str(df2[,3][[1]], max=1) # retrieve using [[ from column returns a list of 12
str(df2[1,], max=1) # returns a data frame of 1 row, models column is list of 1
str(df2[[1,]], max=1) # FAIL 'argument "..2" is missing, with no default'
str(df2[1,"models"], max=1) # returns a list of 1
str(df2[1,"models"][[1]], max=1) # returns a list of 12

# the elements of the parameters and models are accessible in the usual way
# but with the disadvantage of a level of indirection to get from the
parameters to the corresponding models
df2[,-3] # ok
df2[,3] # ok
df2$models # ok
summary(df2$models[[1]]) # ok
summary(df2[1,]$models[[1]]) # ok - needs the [[1]] to unlist the model

# typical functions to use the models and parameters
fn2.1 <- function(x){
a_ply(x, 1, function(df){xx <- rnorm(50); yy <- (df$a * xx +
df$b)^3; zz <- predict(df$models[[1]], newdata=data.frame(x=xx));
print(cor(yy, zz))})
}
fn2.1(df2) # ok

fn2.2 <- function(x){
adply(x, 1, function(df){xx <- rnorm(50); yy <- (df$a * xx +
df$b)^3; zz <- predict(df$models[[1]], newdata=data.frame(x=xx));
data.frame(r=cor(yy, zz))})
}
fn2.2(df2) # FAIL "Error in unlist(xx) : argument not a list" even if
returned data frame is just a constant

fn2.3 <- function(x){
alply(x, 1, function(df){xx <- rnorm(50); yy <- (df$a * xx +
df$b)^3; zz <- predict(df$models[[1]], newdata=data.frame(x=xx));
data.frame(r=cor(yy, zz))})
}
fn2.3(df2) # FAIL "Error in unlist(xx) : argument not a list" creatse
list of output values but appears to die while constructing labels

# I believe a*ply(df, 1, ...) would be the more idiomatic way to
process a data frame one row at a time
# but that's not working for me - so try d*ply instead
fn2.4 <- function(x){
d_ply(x, .(a, b), function(df){xx <- rnorm(50); yy <- (df$a * xx +
df$b)^3; zz <- predict(df$models[[1]], newdata=data.frame(x=xx));
print(cor(yy, zz))})
}
fn2.4(df2) # ok

fn2.5 <- function(x){
ddply(x, .(a, b), function(df){xx <- rnorm(50); yy <- (df$a * xx +
df$b)^3; zz <- predict(df$models[[1]], newdata=data.frame(x=xx));
data.frame(r=cor(yy, zz))})
}
fn2.5(df2) # ok

fn2.6 <- function(x){
m_ply(x, function(a, b, models){xx <- rnorm(50); yy <- (a * xx +
b)^3; zz <- predict(models[[1]], newdata=data.frame(x=xx));
print(cor(yy, zz))})
}
fn2.6(df2) # ok

fn2.7 <- function(x){
mdply(x, function(a, b, models){xx <- rnorm(50); yy <- (a * xx +
b)^3; zz <- predict(models[[1]], newdata=data.frame(x=xx));
data.frame(r=cor(yy, zz))})
}
fn2.7(df2) # FAIL "Error in unlist(xx) : argument not a list"

# try something really simple in plyr
name_rows(df2) # FAIL "Error in unlist(xx) : argument not a list"


##### try it the way adrian baddeley suggested #####
# insert models as a column of a hyperframe
library(spatstat)

# using what I presume is non-idiomatic because I don't yet know what works
df3 <- data.frame(a=1:3, b=4:6) # store the parameters describing some
populations to be modeled
model3 <- alply(df3, 1, function(p){n <- 100; x <- rnorm(n); lm(I(p$a
* x + p$b + rnorm(n)) ~ x)}) # generate a list of models
hf3 <- hyperframe(a=df3$a, b=df3$b, models=model3) # store the list of
models as a column in a hyperframe

# can we access the models as we would expect?
dim(hf3) # ok
names(hf3) # ok
hf3 # ok - it's nice to have an object be printable

str(lm(I(rnorm(10)) ~ rnorm(10)), max=1) # an lm object is a list of 12

hf3[1,3] # retrieve using [ returns a 1x1 hyperframe containing an lm object
class(hf3[1,3]) # yup - it's a hyperframe (and a list)
hf3[1,3][[1]] # returns 1 !!!
hf3[[1,3]] # FAIL "Error in hf3[[1, 3]] : incorrect number of subscripts"

hf3[1,1] # returns a 1x1 hyperframe containing 1
hf3[1,1] + 10 # FAIL "Error in hf3[1, 1] + 10 : non-numeric argument
to binary operator"
hf3[1,] # returns a 3x1 hyperframe containing 1
hf3$a[1] # returns 1
hf3$models[1] # returns an lm object
hf3[1,"models"] # returns a 1x1 hyperframe containing an lm object

# typical functions to use the models and parameters

# can I *_ply over a hyperframe?
# each test is first with a standard frame then second with a hyperframe

a_ply(df1, 1, function(df){print(df$a)}) # ok
a_ply(hf3, 1, function(df){print(df$a)}) # FAIL "Error in
x$env$data[[1L, , drop = TRUE]] : incorrect number of subscripts"

d_ply(df1, .(a, b), function(df){print(df$a)}) # ok
d_ply(hf3, .(a, b), function(df){print(df$a)}) # FAIL "Error in
eval(expr, envir, enclos) : object 'a' not found"

# try something really simple
name_rows(df1) # ok
name_rows(hf3) # FAIL "Error: is.data.frame(df) is not TRUE"

On 1 December 2012 22:12, Ross Gayler <r.ga...@gmail.com> wrote:
> Hi Dennis,
>
> I believe I have now sorted this out to my satisfaction. It *is* possible to
> construct a data.frame with a column containing model fit objects. However,
> most of the techniques for getting the model fit objects into and out of the
> data frame column don't work (contrary to my intuitive expectations). In
> particular, the column has to be wrapped in as.list() to enable the elements
> to be extracted as model fit objects.
>
> The simplest and most reliable approach appears to be what you suggested -
> don't put models in frames. Instead, keep them in lists.
>
> Ross
>
>
> Here is what I tried to arrive at that conclusion.
>
>
> # describe the structure of an entity
> what.am.i <- function(x) {
> plv <- function(label, value){print(label); print(value)}
> plv("STR", str(x, 1))
> plv("LENGTH", length(x))
> plv("CLASS", class(x))
> plv("MODE", mode(x))
> plv("TYPEOF", typeof(x))
> }
>
> # a model
> m <- lm(rnorm(100) ~ runif(100))
> what.am.i(m)
>
> # an empty vector created with c()
> what.am.i(c())
>
> # a vector of models ?
> mvec1 <- c(m, m, m)
> what.am.i(mvec1)
> # Oops! That is a list of length 36 instead of 3
> # c() must decompose m into its top level components before concatenating
>
> # an empty vector created with vector()
> what.am.i(vector(mode="list"))
>
> # a vector of models created with vector() ?
> mvec2 <- vector(mode="list", length=3)
> mvec2[1] <- m; mvec2[2] <- m; mvec2[3] <- m
> what.am.i(mvec2)
> what.am.i(mvec2[1])
> # Oops! That provoked warning messages from the assignments.
> # The result is a list of length 3 but mvec2[1] is not an "lm" object.
>
> # Try wrapping the models in I() and compose with c()
> what.am.i(I(m))
> mvec3 <- c(I(m), I(m), I(m))
> what.am.i(mvec3)
> # Oops! Still a list of length 36
>
> # Try wrapping the models in I() and assign to a vector
> mvec4 <- vector(mode="list", length=3)
> mvec4[1] <- I(m); mvec4[2] <- I(m); mvec4[3] <- I(m)
> what.am.i(mvec4)
> what.am.i(mvec4[1])
> # Oops! That provoked warning messages from the assignments.
> # The result is a list of length 3 but mvec2[1] is not an "lm" object.
> # The I() didn't help
>
> # an empty list
> what.am.i(list())

>> The problem is that model objects are generally lists, and method
>> functions (e.g., summary(), predict() and residuals()) exist for
>> specific types of model objects. For example, summary.glm() is not
>> exactly the same as summary.lm(). Moreover, for a given model object
>> m, summary(m) is a different object than m itself.
>>
>> The advantage of list objects is that each component can be a
>> different type of object with different lengths/dimensions. You can
>> see this by fitting a model object, let's call it m, and then calling
>> str(m). Data frames are more restrictive: each column has the same
>> number of rows, and certain types of objects create problems in data
>> frames (e.g., lists and language objects). The bottom line is that
>> lists are more efficient in terms of storage, but at the cost of
>> increased complexity. The game is learning how to efficiently extract
>> information from lists, and that's where knowing how to write
>> extraction functions becomes useful.
